## Why Servlets? {#sec-03-why-servlets-en}

Implementing, from scratch, a Java program capable of answering HTTP requests would require solving, alone, a set of problems common to any Web server: parsing the incoming HTTP message, handling several connections at once (each in its own thread), controlling the lifecycle of the instances in memory, and packaging all of this in a format an application server knows how to install and start.

A Servlet is a Java class that runs inside a Servlet Container (for instance, Apache Tomcat) and automatically receives all of this work already done:

- HTTP request parsing
- Thread management, one per request
- Management of the Servlet's own lifecycle
- A deployment model of its own, packaged into a `.war` file (Web Application Archive)

The Servlet Container corresponds, in the layered architecture presented in [Chapter 1](cap01.qmd), to the Web Tier: this is where Servlets live, between the client and the business layer.

## The Servlet Lifecycle {#sec-03-lifecycle-en}

When a request is routed to a Servlet, the container always follows the same sequence:

1. If an instance of that Servlet does not yet exist in memory, the container loads the class, creates an instance, and calls the `init()` method
2. For every request received, the container invokes the `service()` method, which dispatches to `doGet()`, `doPost()`, or another method depending on the HTTP verb used, passing it the `request` and `response` objects
3. If the container needs to remove the Servlet (for instance, when the server shuts down), it invokes the `destroy()` method

An important detail follows from this: there is a **single instance** of each Servlet in memory, even with N clients using the same service at once. Each request is handled by a different thread, but all of those threads share the same instance. In practice, this means:

::: {.callout-warning}
## Beware of shared state

Never store data from a specific request in the Servlet's instance attributes: since the instance is shared by all threads, one request can read or overwrite data from another request in progress. Local variables, declared inside `doGet()` or `doPost()`, are safe, because each thread has its own copy.
:::

## From the HTTP Message to the Java Method {#sec-03-http-servlet-mapping-en}

A Servlet is bound to a URL through the `@WebServlet` annotation, which maps a path to the class that will handle it:

```java
@WebServlet("/country")
public class CountryServlet extends HttpServlet {
    // ...
}
```

A request to `http://localhost:8080/country` is thus routed to the `CountryServlet` class. Inside it, the elements of the HTTP message (see [Chapter 1](cap01.qmd)) correspond to concrete methods on the `request` and `response` objects:

| HTTP element | Java access |
|---|---|
| Request headers | `request.getHeader(name)` |
| Parameters (query string or body) | `request.getParameter(name)` |
| Request body (JSON, raw data) | `request.getInputStream()` |
| Writing the response | `response.getWriter()` or `response.getOutputStream()` |

```java
protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) {
    String countryCode = request.getParameter("countrycode");
    // ...
}
```

## Content-Type and the Shape of the Response {#sec-03-content-type-en}

Before writing anything to the response, it is essential to set its `Content-Type`: this header tells the client how to interpret the bytes that follow, whether as an HTML page or as JSON data.

```java
response.setContentType("text/html");
PrintWriter out = response.getWriter();
out.println("<html><body>");
out.println("<h1>Hello João</h1>");
out.println("</body></html>");
```

```java
response.setContentType("application/json");
PrintWriter out = response.getWriter();
out.print("{\"name\":\"João\",\"role\":\"admin\"}");
```

Without a dedicated JSON library, the most direct approach is to build the String manually, taking care to escape internal quotes with `\"`:

```java
String jsonResponse = "{\"country\": \"Portugal\", \"capital\": \"Lisboa\", \"ccode\": \"PT\"}";
out.print(jsonResponse);
out.flush();
```

## A First Servlet: "World Capitals" {#sec-03-first-servlet-en}

Applying what has been presented, a first Servlet can serve as a simple health check for the API:

```java
@WebServlet("/status")
public class StatusServlet extends HttpServlet {
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        response.setContentType("text/plain");
        PrintWriter out = response.getWriter();
        out.print("OK");
    }
}
```

And a second one, already returning fixed data in JSON format, is the first step of the "World Capitals" application used throughout this course:

```java
@WebServlet("/countrycapital")
public class CountryCapitalServlet extends HttpServlet {
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        response.setContentType("application/json");
        PrintWriter out = response.getWriter();

        String jsonResponse = "{\"country\": \"Portugal\", \"capital\": \"Lisboa\", \"ccode\": \"PT\"}";
        out.print(jsonResponse);
        out.flush();
    }
}
```

This Servlet always returns the same country, with the data fixed directly in the code. This is a deliberate simplification: the practical LAB1 picks up exactly at this point, replacing the fixed data with a dedicated data-access object (DAO), preparing the ground for later connecting to a real database server.
